stories.headline: Federal report sets Colorado River conservation targets, asks Upper Basin states to save up to 200,000 acre-feet
stories.summary:
A final environmental impact statement released Friday by the federal government outlines how the Colorado River basin's key reservoirs, including lakes Mead and Powell, will be managed over the next decade. The report sets a conservation target of up to 200,000 acre-feet — roughly 65 billion gallons — to be shared among the four Upper Basin states: Colorado, New Mexico, Wyoming and Utah.

Lower Basin states Arizona, California and Nevada face more severe water cuts, potentially up to 3 million acre-feet under two-year operating plans that will govern reservoir releases and storage. States and tribes will negotiate specific conservation plans every two years through 2036. Secretary of the Interior Doug Burgum said the framework provides flexibility while preserving opportunities for consensus-based solutions.

Colorado officials said Friday they were still reviewing the report and did not respond to questions about the conservation target. The document represents the culmination of a three-year federal planning process and gives state water managers their first firm target to work toward as drought conditions persist across the basin.

stories.headline: Denver police pursuit of carjacking suspect ends in Highway 7 crash, teenage victim seriously injured
stories.summary:
Denver police pursued a suspected carjacker early Friday morning after receiving a report of a vehicle taken with a teenage girl still inside, near the 4700 block of West First Avenue around 5:15 a.m. Officers located the car within minutes and followed it north on Interstate 25 before the suspect exited at Colorado Highway 7 and crashed near Washington Street at approximately 5:36 a.m.

Both the suspect and the victim are 17-year-old males and females, respectively. The female victim sustained what police described as serious injuries. Denver Police spokesman Doug Schepman said the pursuit was authorized because the victim remained inside the vehicle throughout.

Police believe the incident was preceded by an argument among a larger group that had been together, and that the victim and suspect did not know each other. No weapons were involved. Colorado Highway 7 was closed in both directions between I-25 and Washington Street for several hours, with eastbound lanes reopening around 10 a.m.

stories.headline: Preliminary report details how failed helicopter rescue left firefighters trapped in deadly Mesa County blaze
stories.summary:
The U.S. Wildland Fire Service and the U.S. Forest Service have released a preliminary report explaining the sequence of events that led to the deaths of four firefighters during the Knowles Fire near Grand Junction on June 27. The report reveals that five members of the Rifle Interagency Helitack Crew were inserted into the fire area at 9:36 a.m. and were later trapped when a separate lightning-caused ignition rapidly merged with the nearby Snyder and Jones fires under 30-to-50 mph winds.

By 2:56 p.m., crews reported the blaze was nearing their location and a helicopter was dispatched, estimated to arrive within five minutes. At 3:19 p.m., the helicopter was unable to land due to near-zero visibility caused by smoke held at ground level by the high winds, forcing the five firefighters to deploy emergency shelters.

Three firefighters — Emily Barker, Nick Hutcherson and Sydney Watson — were found deceased following the burnover. A fourth, Nathan Matthews, died July 24 from his injuries. The fifth firefighter continues to recover. The Snyder Fire ultimately burned approximately 30,202 acres and is now at 98 percent containment.

stories.headline: National trade group sues Colorado to block statewide free curbside recycling program
stories.summary:
The New Civil Liberties Alliance, representing the National Association of Wholesaler-Distributors, filed a lawsuit Thursday in U.S. District Court in Denver seeking to halt Colorado's Producer Responsibility Program, a state-approved plan that would deliver free curbside recycling to more than 700,000 homes and businesses by 2035. The program, approved in December, is funded through fees charged to companies that create product packaging, including major corporations such as Amazon, Coca-Cola and General Mills.

The lawsuit alleges the program is administered by the Circular Action Alliance — a body made up of packaging industry representatives — which plaintiffs say is controlled by large companies that compete against smaller distributors. The suit contends that small businesses are forced to become dues-paying members of the alliance and forfeit their right to challenge its fee decisions in court, citing violations of the First and Fourteenth amendments.

Attorneys are asking a federal judge for a preliminary injunction to pause the program while litigation proceeds. A similar suit was filed in March by the Independent Lubricant Manufacturers Association on related grounds. The first round of fees was due June 1, and initial curbside programs are expected to launch later this year or in early 2027.

stories.headline: Colorado drought forces farmers to fallow unprecedented shares of cropland ahead of winter
stories.summary:
Colorado farmers on the Front Range are fallowing record portions of their land this season as historic drought drains irrigation canals and depletes reservoirs. Jim Magnuson, who operates a family farm in Eaton that dates to 1908, said he has left 25 percent of his acreage unplanted for the first time ever, substituting drought-tolerant millet and sorghum on a portion of the rest. The low snowpack has sharply reduced flows in the Cache la Poudre River, which feeds the canals his farm depends on.

Robert Sakata, an agricultural water policy adviser for the Colorado Department of Agriculture whose family farms in Brighton, chose to fallow 40 percent of his acreage this season, calling it an immediate 40 percent pay cut while fixed costs like property taxes remain unchanged. His operation relies on direct-flow water rights from the South Platte River, which has seen drastically reduced flows this year.

The fallowing decisions will ripple through the livestock sector as well, with less corn silage and hay available for cattle and dairy operations this winter. Farmers warn that without significant mountain snowpack next winter, reservoirs will not refill and the 2027 growing season could face equal or greater water shortages.

stories.headline: Heat advisory issued for Denver metro as temperatures expected to approach 100 degrees this weekend
stories.summary:
The National Weather Service has issued a heat advisory for the I-25 urban corridor, including Denver and the Greeley area, as afternoon high temperatures are forecast to reach approximately 100 degrees Sunday, with similarly elevated readings expected through Monday. Friday's high reached 90 degrees, with a 40 percent chance of evening thunderstorms arriving around 4 p.m.

The weekend heat will mark the fourth consecutive day of afternoon rain chances before the pattern shifts to drier, hotter conditions. Forecasters are urging residents to seek shade, stay hydrated and avoid strenuous outdoor activity during peak afternoon heat hours.

The forecast temperatures are near record-breaking levels for the Denver metro area. Officials advise residents to check on elderly neighbors and avoid leaving children or pets in vehicles.

stories.headline: Denver International Airport briefly shut down over unattended bag, quickly cleared by bomb squad
stories.summary:
Denver International Airport closed a portion of its terminal Friday evening after a police dog alerted to an unattended bag flagged as a possible security threat. DIA officials shut down Level 6 West at approximately 5:32 p.m., affecting the west security checkpoint, departures area and United Airlines check-in counters.

The Denver Police Department's bomb squad responded and cleared the bag shortly before 7 p.m., after which airport officials announced that operations were returning to normal. No explosive device was found.

The brief closure caused disruptions for travelers during an early-evening peak travel period. Airport officials communicated updates to passengers via email throughout the incident.

stories.headline: Odyssey Italian Restaurant reopens in Capitol Hill after fire, plans second location in Uptown
stories.summary:
Odyssey Italian Restaurant has reopened in Denver's Capitol Hill neighborhood following a February fire that closed the 17-year-old establishment for more than six months. Owners Jason Alfonso and Hallie Thomas completed a kitchen remodel, installed a new grill and refurbished the dining rooms while retaining the restaurant's original layout and decor in the century-old building they own.

The reopening comes amid separate hardship for the owners' other restaurant, Ollie & Park's in Uptown, which was destroyed in May when a U-Haul truck crashed into the building. Rather than rebuild Ollie & Park's, the owners plan to convert the repaired space into a second Odyssey location, to be called Odyssey Uptown, with construction expected to begin next month pending installation of replacement windows.

General manager Ned Nichols said approximately 80 percent of Odyssey's front-of-house staff returned, and the restaurant has expanded its menu to include grilled Colorado lamb, pork, filet mignon and other entrees made possible by the new kitchen equipment. Nichols credited building ownership as the key factor allowing the restaurant to survive the fire, saying a rented space would have made reopening financially impossible.

stories.headline: Billionaire Bill Koch's Aspen estate sells for $35.52 million at auction, down sharply from $125 million asking price
stories.summary:
Billionaire Bill Koch's 52-acre estate in Aspen has sold for $35.52 million at auction after the property spent years on the market with an asking price of $125 million. The steep discount represents a reduction of more than 70 percent from the original listing.

The sale of the Elk Mountain Lodge property underscores the continued softening of the ultra-luxury mountain real estate market in Colorado, even as Aspen remains among the most expensive resort communities in the country. Koch, an energy and America's Cup sailing figure, had listed the property at a price that would have made it among the most expensive residential sales in Colorado history.

Details on the buyer were not immediately disclosed. The auction outcome highlights how even trophy properties in coveted Colorado mountain locations face significant price discovery challenges when initial asking prices are set far above market-clearing levels.

stories.headline: Broncos notebook: Ben Powers takes 50 percent pay cut, Garett Bolles lands at No. 42 on NFL Top 100
stories.summary:
Denver Broncos guard Ben Powers has agreed to a restructured one-year deal worth $6 million, with $5 million guaranteed, cutting his previous nonguaranteed $12.49 million salary roughly in half. Powers, who missed nine games in 2025 with a torn biceps and played through a Lisfranc foot injury in the playoffs, retains a salary-cap number of $10.6 million due to prorated money from his original four-year, $52 million contract.

Head coach Sean Payton said Powers is performing well in training camp and is viewed as a starter, though competition from Alex Palczewski — who started 10 games during Powers' absence last season — will continue through the preseason. Payton noted competition exists throughout the roster at multiple positions including quarterback and tight end.

Left tackle Garett Bolles, who earned his first-team All-Pro selection last season, was revealed at No. 42 on the NFL Top 100 list, which is voted on by players. The ranking marks the highest of Bolles' 10-year career, surpassing his previous best of No. 82 in 2021.

stories.headline: Broncos linebacker Alex Singleton returns to training camp with renewed perspective after cancer surgery
stories.summary:
Denver Broncos linebacker Alex Singleton, 32, spoke with local media at training camp Friday for the first time since his November 2025 announcement that he had undergone surgery to remove a cancerous testicular tumor. The cancer was detected through an NFL drug test that flagged elevated levels of the hormone human chorionic gonadotropin, and the operation was successful with no spread of the disease.

Singleton returned to play 16 regular-season games in 2025, leading the Broncos in tackles for the third time in four seasons, and recorded 26 additional stops in two playoff games. He said the experience has shaped a compartmentalized approach to daily life, describing a philosophy of focusing on what is immediately in front of him rather than looking ahead.

The linebacker's path to the NFL was itself unconventional, including stints with three NFL teams that released him before he played a game, three productive seasons in the Canadian Football League, and a torn ACL in 2024 that cost him most of that season. Singleton has led Denver in tackles in each of his first three healthy seasons with the team.

stories.headline: Garth Brooks adds two more Denver concerts after initial Ball Arena shows sell out instantly
stories.summary:
Country music star Garth Brooks has added a Sunday matinee and evening performance on Sept. 6 at Ball Arena in Denver after his previously announced Friday and Saturday shows on Sept. 4 and 5 sold out immediately. The four-show Denver run is part of his "Blame It On My Roots" tour, his first Denver appearance since a June 2019 concert at Empower Field at Mile High.

Tickets for the new shows went on sale Saturday morning through Ticketmaster at a flat price of $155.25 per seat in every section of the arena, a format Brooks calls "one fair price." The pricing model, which eliminates tiered seat pricing, is intended to improve access for fans in all sections and reduce resale market activity, according to promoters.

All tickets are sold with an eight-ticket per purchase limit, with no pre-sales or advance box office sales. The Denver shows feature both end-stage and in-the-round seating configurations.

topStory.headline: Death Toll From Southwestern Japan Earthquake Rises to 34 as Rescue Operations Enter Fourth Day
topStory.summary:
A magnitude 7.1 earthquake that struck Japan's southern main island of Kyushu on Tuesday has killed at least 34 people, with one additional death still under investigation, the Kumamoto prefectural government confirmed Friday. The quake damaged more than 1,500 buildings, including 179 that were destroyed, and left tens of thousands of residents without water and electricity across the region.

Nearly half of the confirmed deaths were tied to two major incidents: the collapse of a chimney at a Nippon Paper Industries factory in the Yatsushiro area, where nine people were killed and 11 rescued before the search operation concluded, and an explosion at an Aeon Mall shopping center in the town of Kashima, where seven people were confirmed dead and 11 were rescued from the partially collapsed structure. The mall had been crowded with roughly 3,000 shoppers when the quake struck; they were evacuated to a parking lot before a blast tore through a section where staff remained.

Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged authorities to secure water supplies by doing 'whatever it takes' and called for close coordination between the military and relevant agencies. As of Friday afternoon, more than 79,000 homes remained without tap water and over 2,700 were still without electricity, though the local power company said full restoration of power was achieved by Friday evening. Officials also warned of a fuel shortage caused by disabled gas stations and disrupted deliveries, leaving many evacuees struggling to run air conditioning in their vehicles amid temperatures approaching 36 degrees Celsius.

More than 9,000 people were sheltering in evacuation centers as of Friday, where authorities were adding power sources to provide air conditioning in response to concerns about heat-related illness. Japanese officials described Friday afternoon as a critical threshold in rescue efforts, noting that survival chances for those trapped under debris typically decline after the first 72 hours. Smaller-scale searches continued at collapsed houses in southern Kumamoto, and it remained unclear how many people were still missing.

The earthquake is the deadliest to strike Kumamoto prefecture in a decade. A 2016 quake in the same region killed 275 people and remains the benchmark for seismic disaster response in southwestern Japan, which sits in one of the world's most active earthquake zones. Prime Minister Takaichi also urged residents to remain vigilant for strong aftershocks as relief and recovery operations continued.
